copy: POV: You signed your kid up for guitar lessons and now they won't stop playing the first 7 notes of Mario Bros. You're welcome.
imageNote: Photo of a young student mid-shred with a big grin, or a staged "parent covering ears" shot

copy: Your practice routine is not "playing the same song you already know for 20 minutes." That's a concert. Practice means the stuff that's hard. Here's a 10-minute routine that actually moves the needle.
imageNote: Carousel: Slide 1 - "Your practice routine needs work." Slide 2 - 2 min scales/warmup, Slide 3 - 3 min trouble spots, Slide 4 - 3 min new material, Slide 5 - 2 min play something fun. Slide 6 - "That's it. 10 minutes. No excuses."

copy: Our teachers played a show last weekend. Your kid's piano teacher was headlining a jazz set at 11pm on Saturday. Most studios can't say that.
imageNote: Photo of a BLE teacher performing live at a gig

copy: Things you hear walking down the hallway at BLE: a 7-year-old nailing a drum fill, a teenager belting Adele, someone's first piano chord ever, and at least one guitar solo that goes way too hard.
imageNote: Reel: Quick cuts of different lesson rooms, each with a few seconds of audio. End with a teacher bobbing their head approvingly.

copy: Six months ago this kid could barely hold a pick. Last Saturday he played his first solo in front of 50 people and didn't even flinch. We're not crying, you're crying. OK fine we're all crying.
imageNote: Photo of student performing at a recital, crowd visible

copy: Hot take: Practicing 10 minutes a day beats practicing 2 hours on Sunday. Your brain learns through repetition, not marathon sessions. Set a timer. Play every day. Watch what happens.
Meet [Teacher Name], our drum instructor. He's toured with [band/artist], played on actual albums you've heard, and now he's teaching your 8-year-old paradiddles. The range is unmatched.
imageNote: Photo of drum teacher at the kit, or split image: performing live vs. teaching a young student

copy: When your student asks "can I try something?" and then plays something that wasn't even in the lesson plan. The best moments aren't scripted.
imageNote: Reel: Teacher reacting with genuine surprise/pride. Student plays something unexpected. Teacher's face says it all.

copy: If your kid says "I already practiced" and you didn't hear anything... they did not practice. Source: every music teacher ever.

Studio tour but make it real. Here's the room where beginners have their first "I actually did it" moment. Here's where the advanced kids pretend they're at Madison Square Garden. Here's the water cooler where parents bond over recital anxiety.
imageNote: Reel: Casual, handheld walkthrough of the studio with text overlays for each room

copy: The difference between a music teacher and a working musician who teaches? One shows you how to play a chord. The other shows you how that chord feels on stage at midnight in front of a crowd. All our teachers are the second kind.
imageNote: Photo of teacher in a teaching moment, or a collage of teachers performing vs. teaching

copy: Started voice lessons because she was too shy to sing in front of her family. Just performed her first solo at the showcase. Her mom's reaction in the second pic is everything.
imageNote: Photo 1: Student singing on stage. Photo 2: Parent in audience visibly emotional

copy:
Mistakes parents make about practice (with love):
1. Asking "did you practice?" instead of practicing WITH them
2. Expecting perfection instead of progress
3. Comparing to the kid who's been playing 3 years longer
4. Turning it into a punishment

You're doing great. Just keep showing up.
imageNote: Carousel: Each slide is one mistake with a fun illustration or meme-style graphic. Final slide is encouraging.

copy: Our voice teacher's Spotify has more streams than most people's entire playlists. She also gets genuinely hyped when a 6-year-old hits their first high note. That combo is hard to find.
imageNote: Photo of voice teacher with students, or a screenshot of their Spotify artist page next to a teaching photo

copy: What our front desk sees every day: kids running in excited, kids walking out playing air guitar, at least one parent secretly hoping their kid becomes famous, and a truly unhinged amount of high fives.
imageNote: Reel: Montage from a camera near the front desk. Kids arriving, leaving, celebrating. Staff giving high fives.

copy: Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. If you can't play it slow, you definitely can't play it fast. Drop the tempo, nail the notes, then speed up. Every pro does this. Every single one.
Asked our guitar teacher what he listens to on his day off. Got a playlist that goes from Hendrix to Hozier to anime soundtracks. This is the kind of range your kid gets access to.
imageNote: Screenshot of an eclectic playlist or photo of guitar teacher with headphones

copy: Adult student alert. He started piano at 42 because "it was on my bucket list." Three months in, he's playing songs for his wife at home. Never too late, never too old, never too busy.
imageNote: Photo of adult student at the piano, or candid shot during lesson

copy: The metronome is not your enemy. It's the friend who tells you the truth when no one else will. Use it. Hate it. Become best friends with it. In that order.

Fun fact: Our piano teacher studied at [conservatory/university] and could've gone the stuffy classical route. Instead she teaches kids in Friendswood how to play Coldplay and movie soundtracks because she thinks music should be fun. We agree.
imageNote: Photo of piano teacher mid-lesson, smiling

copy: First lesson vs. six months later. Same kid. Same guitar. Completely different energy. This is why we do what we do.
imageNote: Reel: Split screen or before/after. First lesson: tentative, unsure. Six months later: confident, playing a full song.

copy:
How to actually read music (without wanting to quit):
Step 1 - Stop panicking, it's just dots on lines.
Step 2 - Learn the spaces first (FACE, you already know it).
Step 3 - Then the lines (Every Good Boy Does Fine).
Step 4 - Practice reading 2 minutes a day.
Step 5 - Realize it's way easier than you thought.
imageNote: Carousel with simple, clean graphics for each step. Not cluttered. Meme-friendly aesthetic.

copy: Recital prep week is basically the Super Bowl around here. Teachers rehearsing, students buzzing, someone is definitely stress-eating donuts in the break room. We wouldn't have it any other way.
imageNote: Photo of bustling studio during recital prep - teachers setting up, students warming up

copy: She told her mom she wanted to play violin "because it sounds like a movie." Four months later she played the theme from Schindler's List at the showcase. She's 9. We can't even.
imageNote: Photo of young violin student performing

copy: "Where do you find your teachers?" Playing gigs around Houston. Our hiring process is basically: Are you insanely talented? Do you actually like kids? Can you make a lesson feel like hanging out? If yes to all three, welcome aboard.
Your kid doesn't need to practice for an hour. They need to practice with focus. Five focused minutes beats thirty minutes of noodling around. Quality over quantity. Always.
He came in wanting to learn one song for his girlfriend. He learned the song. He also learned 15 more because turns out he actually loves playing guitar. Tale as old as time.
imageNote: Photo of teen/young adult student playing guitar, or a candid lesson shot
